hints: Count how many lone pairs each ligand can donate at the same time, start with the small ligands $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{CN}^-$ which each have only one donor atom.
Compare $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ which has two O donor atoms with $\text{EDTA}^{4-}$ which has six donor atoms (2 N plus 4 O).
walkthrough:
Link the name to the number of teeth**
Think of dentate as meaning toothed, like how many teeth bite onto the metal. One donor atom biting once is monodentate, two donor atoms biting twice is bidentate, and many donor atoms is polydentate.

Sort the four ligands**
$\text{NH}_3$ donates only the lone pair on N, so one dative bond, monodentate. $\text{CN}^-$ donates only the lone pair on C (or N), so monodentate. $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$, ethanedioate, has two O atoms that can bond at once, so bidentate. $\text{EDTA}^{4-}$ wraps round with six donor atoms, so polydentate.

Final answer: $\text{NH}_3$ = monodentate
$\text{EDTA}^{4-}$ = polydentate
$\text{CN}^-$ = monodentate
$\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ = bidentate

hints: Use the prefix tri in tridentate to tell you the number, then link it to what a ligand does with its lone pairs.
walkthrough:
Decode the word tridentate**
Tri means three, and dentate means donor sites binding to the metal. So picture one single ligand molecule attaching at three points at once, donating three separate lone pairs to form three dative bonds to the same central $\text{M}^{n+}$ ion.
Final answer: A ligand that donates three lone pairs to the central metal ion, forming three dative bonds.

hints: Look at the formula $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ and spot how many nitrogen atoms are present that each carry a lone pair.
walkthrough:
Find the three binding teeth**
Write out the molecule: $\text{H}_2\text{N-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-NH-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-NH}_2$. You can see three separate N atoms, two $\text{-NH}_2$ ends and one $\text{-NH-}$ in the middle. Each N has a lone pair available, so each N donates its lone pair to form a dative bond, giving three bonds in total.
Final answer: It bonds through the lone pair on each of the three N atoms / amine groups.

hints: In octahedral $[\text{Ni}(en)_2(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2]^{2+}$, think where the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands sit, opposite each other at $180^{\circ}$ in trans or next to each other at $90^{\circ}$ in cis, and how that affects cancellation of dipoles.
walkthrough:
Picture the symmetry**
Focus only on the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands, because the two $en$ ligands are the same in each case. In the trans form the two $\text{O-Ni-O}$ bonds point in exactly opposite directions, so their bond dipoles cancel and the complex has no overall dipole, it is non-polar. In both cis forms the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands are at $90^{\circ}$, side by side, so the dipoles cannot cancel and the complex has a permanent dipole, it is polar.

Final answer: trans isomer = non-polar
cis isomer 1 = polar
cis isomer 2 = polar

hints: If both structures are cis but they are still different and cannot be superimposed, recall the type of stereoisomerism that gives non-superimposable mirror images.
walkthrough:
See why two cis forms exist**
With bidentate $en$, the cis arrangement can wrap round the octahedron in two mirror image ways, like left handed and right handed propellers. They have the same formula and the same cis $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ positions, but one cannot be placed exactly on top of the other. That is optical isomerism, so the pair are enantiomers which rotate plane polarised light in opposite directions.
Final answer: They are optical isomers / enantiomers, non-superimposable mirror images of each other.
